title: Latency leak mitigations and rolling backoff strategy
creator: Lina Park
description: Post-incident analysis of a multi-region tail-latency surge that briefly pushed the public text-generation SLO past the P99 threshold. The incident involved cascading circuit activations, asymmetric failover, and load-shedding mismatch across regions after a routing rule change and an uneven shard warm-up. This ticket collects timeline, root cause analysis, mitigations applied during the event, and a prioritized set of action items to prevent recurrence and reduce blast radius.
incident_summary: On 2026-02-28 14:22 UTC we received a P99 latency alert for the text-generation API for customers routed through the EU region. Within 6 minutes, tail latency increased in multiple regions as fallback routing shifted traffic unevenly; automated circuit breakers triggered across heterogeneous pools and caused oscillatory failovers. The SLO (P99 < 250ms) was missed for a 18-minute window for high-traffic tenants before mitigations stabilized traffic. No data loss or customer data exposure occurred.
timeline: 2026-02-28 14:20 UTC — small customer cache warmup job finished unusually slowly after a maintenance window in eu-west-1
2026-02-28 14:22 UTC — SLO alert: eu-west-1 P99 breached 320ms
2026-02-28 14:24 UTC — traffic auto-routed to eu-central-1 and us-west-2; eu-central experienced a 2x request spike
2026-02-28 14:26 UTC — circuit-breaker hysteresis in eu-central misestimated backend healthy capacity and opened, shedding requests
2026-02-28 14:28 UTC — circuit openings in fallback regions forced secondary fallbacks to additional pools leading to oscillation
2026-02-28 14:32 UTC — on-call initiated manual circuit smoothing and paused new canary routing change rolled out earlier that day
2026-02-28 14:38 UTC — temporary global sticky-affinity rule applied to pin in-flight sessions to origin regions to reduce fanout
2026-02-28 14:40 UTC — capacity burst added to dedicated pools and KV cache prewarm triggered via emergency path
2026-02-28 14:58 UTC — P99 returned below SLO for majority of tenants; incident declared mitigated
2026-02-28 15:10 UTC — close monitoring for 2 hours; no further regressions observed
detection: Primary detection was automated SLO alerts firing on global monitoring (P99 > 250ms). Secondary signals: elevated circuit-open rates in the control plane, increase in fallback counts, and a surge in cross-region egress in traffic metrics. On-call paged from alert runbook and escalated to the resilience squad.
root_cause: A confluence of three factors: (1) a rolling change to routing weights and canary for a new sticky-affinity algorithm was active with insufficient backpressure simulation; (2) a delayed KV cache warmup in eu-west-1 caused that region to appear unhealthy causing upstream routing to overflow other regions; (3) circuit-breaker hysteresis parameters (open/half-open timings and capacity estimation) were tuned conservatively after a prior incident and amplified oscillation when multiple pools shared fallback targets. The orchestration layer lacked per-tenant fanout caps during emergency failover, which increased blast radius.
impact: SLO breach for P99 (text-generation) for 18 minutes for ~12% of production traffic; increased token latency for several enterprise tenants, triggering partial degraded UX. No request data loss. Estimated customer impact: medium (service interruption but recovery within 30 minutes). Internal SLA blips for a small number of Dedicated customers; account success alerted.
immediate_mitigation: paused the sticky-affinity canary rollouts and reverted routing weight change at 14:32 UTC
applied a temporary sticky-affinity pin to avoid excessive fanout for in-flight sessions at 14:38 UTC
increased burst capacity on dedicated pools and triggered emergency KV cache prewarm jobs at 14:40 UTC
manually smoothed circuit breaker transitions by forcing longer half-open windows on affected pools to reduce thrash
long_term_remediations: Introduce per-tenant and per-route fanout caps in the orchestration layer to limit cross-region amplification
Revise circuit-breaker hysteresis defaults and add adaptive capacity estimation that uses short-term moving averages instead of single-sample signals
Add mandatory canary chaos tests for routing weight and affinity changes that include failover simulations and backpressure scenarios
Implement proactive KV cache warming hooks for region failover paths and ensure cache-warm metrics are part of deployment gating
Create an emergency routing circuit that allows graceful degraded responses (lower token-per-second limits) instead of full rejection during multi-region overload
action_items: ENG-701789 — Implement per-tenant fanout ceiling in router (owner: Marco Alvarez; estimate: 8)
ENG-702010 — Circuit hysteresis tune: replace fixed timers with adaptive estimator + unit tests (owner: Priya Natarajan; estimate: 5)
ENG-702115 — KV cache prewarm: add cross-region prewarm hook and gate (owner: Jonas Peters; estimate: 3)
ENG-702345 — Canary safety harness: add backpressure/failover simulation to canary pipeline (owner: Zoe Kim; estimate: 5)
ENG-702900 — Runbook update: add diagnostic checklist for multi-region SLO breaches and operator quick actions (owner: Lina Park; estimate: 2)
ENG-703001 — Console dashboard: surface circuit-open rates, fallback counts, and fanout heatmap per region (owner: DevOps Squad; estimate: 5)
ENG-703200 — Add local throttling path to return degraded token-limited responses before tripping circuit (owner: Reliability ML; estimate: 8)
post_incident_notes: We observed that small timing parameter changes to circuit hysteresis can have outsized global effects when combined with routing weight shifts. The orchestration layer's current lack of explicit per-tenant blast radius controls is the primary product gap. Teams should treat routing-affinity changes as high-risk and gate them behind canary simulations that include failover load patterns.
